article.title: Southwest's 2025 fuel-hedge exit did not end the expense clock
article.dek: Southwest's July 2025 filing separates the cash from closing hedges from premium expense still awaiting recognition through 2027.
article.search_title: Southwest's 2025 fuel-hedge exit: cash versus expense
article.meta_description: Southwest's Q2 2025 fuel-hedge exit brought cash proceeds, while premium expense remained deferred. The filing explains the different accounting clocks.
article.social_hook: Southwest closed its fuel hedges in Q2 2025. Why did its filing still point to premium expense through 2027?
article.substack_body_markdown:
Southwest closed its remaining fuel hedges in Q2 2025, yet the accounting did not finish with the contracts. Its [[CITE:SOURCE_1|July 24, 2025 Form 10-Q]] described premium expense still to enter fuel costs through 2027 as the originally forecast transactions occur. For a reader comparing fuel costs, the distinction matters: an expense tied to an old hedge does not, by itself, establish that a new hedge exists. [[SOURCE:SOURCE_1]]

## One closure, three clocks

In Q2 2025, Southwest received approximately $40 million from closing its remaining fuel hedges. The filing said those proceeds would reduce future premium costs. [[SOURCE:SOURCE_1]]

Southwest recorded approximately $36 million of fuel-hedging premium expense in Q2 2025, including terminated positions. That amount moved from accumulated other comprehensive income (AOCI) into fuel and oil expense. In this disclosure, AOCI held premium costs awaiting recognition in the income statement. [[SOURCE:SOURCE_1]]

At June 30, 2025, approximately $209 million remained in AOCI, excluding tax and net of termination proceeds, for reclassification to fuel expense through end-2027 as the originally forecast transactions occur. [[SOURCE:SOURCE_1]]

## Why expense outlasts the contracts

Closing the contracts removed the hedge assets; the filing tied later premium expense to the originally forecast transactions. Capital Chronicle's analysis is that an accounting tail can outlive the portfolio. [[SOURCE:SOURCE_1]]

The practical consequence is to read each amount against its own label and date. One describes money received, another describes expense recognized during a quarter, and the third describes a deferred balance. Adding them into a single exit cost would erase those distinctions. [[SOURCE:SOURCE_1]]

The $209 million balance already incorporated the termination proceeds. Subtracting the $40 million again would count the same offset twice. The $36 million describes the quarter's premium expense, including terminated positions; the passage does not assign the entire amount to the act of closing the book. [[SOURCE:SOURCE_1]]

## What the filing cannot settle

Deferred expense is not a verdict on whether the hedge exit was economically sound. This passage explains accounting timing; it does not measure the contracts' overall benefit or establish how the exit changed subsequent earnings. [[SOURCE:SOURCE_1]]

To test the continuing accounting story, look for later company disclosures showing how the deferred balance moved and whether new contracts were added. This filing alone cannot establish the current hedge policy. [[SOURCE:SOURCE_1]]

That leaves a useful reading rule: identify when the contracts ended, when cash changed hands and when an expense reached earnings before interpreting a hedge-related fuel-cost number. Southwest's 2025 disclosure answers the timing question without settling every question about the decision's economics. [[SOURCE:SOURCE_1]]

Analysis, not financial advice. Readers decide whether to trade. [[SOURCE:SOURCE_1]]

A later expense entry can reflect earlier premiums without proving new contracts, but that accounting distinction also does not prove that fuel-price risk disappeared, that the closure saved money overall or that any later earnings outcome was caused by it. visual_editorial_decision.editorial_thesis: Southwest's Q2 2025 hedge exit shows why closing contracts and finishing their effect on reported expenses are separate events. The cash received on closure, premium expense recognized that quarter and premium expense deferred in AOCI answer different questions. Reading them on their own clocks avoids treating a closed portfolio as a completed income-statement story, double-counting the proceeds or mistaking an accounting balance for a fresh cash bill.

material_claim_bindings.claim_text: Southwest's 2025 fuel-hedge exit did not end the expense clock
material_claim_bindings.support_excerpt: During second quarter 2025, the Company terminated its remaining portfolio of fuel hedging contracts, which were scheduled to settle through 2027, to effectively close its fuel hedging portfolio. This resulted in the derecognition of all remaining related hedge assets in the unaudited Condensed Consolidated Balance Sheet. The cash proceeds from this transaction totaled approximately $40 million, which will reduce future premium costs. Approximately $36 million was reclassified from Accumulated Other Comprehensive Income ("AOCI") and recognized as an increase to Fuel and oil expense within the unaudited Condensed Consolidated Statement of Comprehensive Income during second quarter 2025, all of which is characterized as premium expense from fuel hedging activities, including amounts associated with terminated fuel hedge positions. As of June 30, 2025, approximately $209 million remained in AOCI related to these closed positions. This balance in AOCI does not include any tax impact, will also be characterized as premium expense and similarly reclassified as an increase to Fuel and oil expense in future periods when the originally forecasted transactions occur (through the end of 2027), and is net of the impact of the cash proceeds from the hedge terminations.
